items.title: Identifying and targeting the Mg-Fe-PmrAB regulatory circuit reverses phosphate starvation-driven polymyxin tolerance in Enterobacteriaceae
items.summary: Phosphate (Pi) scarcity, a pervasive stressor prevalent in bacterial infections and dysbiotic host environments, potently alters antimicrobial susceptibility against cationic antibiotics like polymyxins across diverse bacterial taxa. While established Pi depletion-induced antimicrobial tolerance mechanisms often involve membrane phospholipid remodelling, Enterobacteriaceae largely lack these pathways, leaving the mechanism underlying their adaptation to Pi scarcity unresolved. Here, we reveal that Pi limitation robustly induces polymyxin tolerance in Enterobacteriaceae through 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose (L-Ara4N) modification of the Gram-negative outer membrane component lipid A, reflecting a distinct adaptive strategy. This modification is driven by strong arn operon induction, mediated by the PmrAB two-component system. We discover that Pi depletion triggers cellular Mg2+ release, prompting compensatory Fe3+ mobilization to the cell envelope that directly activates PmrAB.
items.author: ZHANG, G., Deng, Z., JIANG, J. et al.

items.title: Environmental DNA reveals biotic homogenization alongside elevated native and non-native species richness in marinas, supporting an ecological portuarization syndrome
items.summary: The global expansion of ports has created novel marine urban ecosystems that remain understudied. Recent evidence suggests that ports promote distinct evolutionary trajectories due to their unique environmental conditions and the continuous introduction of non-indigenous species (NIS), a phenomenon previously coined the `biological portuarization syndrome`. In this study, we examine the ecological dimension of this concept by using environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding, to compare animal assemblages in 12 recreational ports (i.e., marinas) with those found in adjacent natural habitats in the north-western Mediterranean Sea. By combining three markers, we identified 536 species belonging to 18 phyla, including 50 species classified as non-indigenous or cryptogenic based on previous records from traditional surveys.
items.author: Lilli, G., Caillarec-Joly, A., Violet, C. et al.

items.title: Scalable methylome-transcriptome profiling resolves clonal organization in human hematopoiesis
items.summary: Understanding human tissue maintenance and remodeling requires linking clonal ancestry to molecular state, yet scalable joint measurement remains challenging. Here, we introduce Droplet-MT and an integrated computational workflow for joint transcriptome and methylome profiling at ~10,000 cells per library. Methylation epimutations enable mutation-independent clonal reconstruction from high-coverage methylomes, while reference-based label transfer assigns cells to established clones at ~0.2% CpG coverage, reducing sequencing cost. Clone-aggregated somatic variants provide genetic annotation without additional single-cell genotyping. Across ~21,000 paired profiles from healthy blood and longitudinal acute myeloid leukemia, we resolved small and expanded clones with heterogeneous lineage output. In leukemia, the framework distinguished changes in malignant clonal abundance, state remodeling within persistent clones, and recovery of healthy polyclonal hematopoiesis.
items.author: Shao, J., Chen, M., Liu, Y. et al.

items.title: Kinship, acoustic signaling, and socio-spatial structure shape shared decisions and social influence in white-nosed coatis
items.summary: When individual preferences for collective outcomes diverge, cohesive animal groups often coalesce on the majority opinion. However, majority-based decision rules may be counterbalanced by other factors, particularly in heterogeneous groups with differentiated social relationships, and these factors could produce inequality in social influence. We used multi-sensor tracking collars to collect detailed and simultaneous data on the movements and vocalizations of almost all members of three wild white-nosed coati (Nasua narica) groups, and analyzed 2,401 individual decisions between conflicting travel directions that were indicated by acoustically signaling groupmates. Decision-making was shared: individuals favored directions that had majority support, and we found evidence that they used acoustic signals and movement cues to infer majority support.
items.author: Winans, J. C., Grout, E. M., Ortega, J. et al.

items.title: Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics reveals selective organization of α-synuclein inclusions
items.summary: -Synuclein inclusions, the lesions typical of Parkinson's disease, have been interpreted as protective deposits, toxic species or failed degradation products, each predicting a different composition and correlating that enrichment with neuron dysfunction and eventual degeneration. Distinguishing them requires measuring what an inclusion concentrates relative to the cell that built it. Here we developed Aggregate Deep Visual Proteomics, which uses ultrasensitive mass spectrometry to profile laser-microdissected inclusions against the remainder of the same cell or a matched host. In HEK293 cells, iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons and post-mortem patient brain, each inclusion concentrated a selective subset of its cell's proteome, independent of abundance and dominated by membrane, in neurons largely presynaptic.
items.author: Oeller, M., Vasconez Grunauer, S., Sitron, C. S. et al.

items.title: Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning: A Stability-Constrained Framework for Molecularly Enhanced Survival Prediction in Lung Adenocarcinoma
items.summary: Accurate survival prediction in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains challenging because high-dimensional molecular data can introduce overfitting and unstable feature selection. We developed Clinical-Anchored Incremental Survival Learning (CAISL), a framework that integrates a sparse molecular risk correction with a clinical baseline to improve prognostic discrimination while constraining model complexity and prediction variability. CAISL was evaluated using The Cancer Genome Atlas LUAD cohort comprising 470 patients and 119 observed deaths. Performance was compared with clinical Cox, molecular-only, and unanchored multimodal models using five independently seeded, event-stratified five-fold cross-validation runs. CAISL achieved a mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.7246, compared with 0.6970 for clinical Cox, yielding an absolute improvement of 0.0276 (95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 0.005 to 0.050).
items.author: Shringarpure, P., Divakar, S., Khobragade, S.

items.title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
items.summary: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In two participants, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in adjacent stained sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73).
items.author: Ota, K., Chen, T.-H., Yamaguchi, T. et al.

items.title: Genomic prediction of resistance to Phytophthora megakarya in cacao from a sparse host-pathogen screen
items.summary: Black pod rot caused by Phytophthora megakarya is a major disease impacting cacao (Theobroma cacao L.) production in West Africa. Resistance is influenced by genetic variation in both host and pathogen populations. While genomic prediction approaches have been widely applied in plant breeding, most studies incorporate only host genomic information. The value of explicitly modeling pathogen genomic relatedness in quantitative disease prediction remains largely unknown. We genotyped 947 clones from the International Cacao Collection at CATIE using a 10K-SNP panel and characterized 67 P. megakarya isolates by sequencing 3,505 virulence-associated genes and 2,774 SNP loci. Cacao clones were extensively admixed, while isolates formed three geographically structured subpopulations.
items.author: Schlathoelter, I., Gitto, A. J., Arciniegas, A. L. et al.

items.title: Gene regulatory architecture in antibiotic resistance is optimized for specific dynamic regimens
items.summary: Cellular responses to antibiotics face a fundamental trade-off: resistance must be deployed quickly enough to prevent the accumulation of drug inside the cell, but expression of resistance genes is costly in the absence of the drug. Therefore, antibiotic responses are typically regulated, controlling not only whether resistance is expressed, but also when, how strongly, and for how long. These regulatory strategies are implemented through the strength and arrangement of promoters and operators. However, it is still not clear how the dynamics of drug exposure select for specific regulatory strategies. Here, we develop a dynamical model of a typical antibiotic response, where a transcriptional repressor senses the drug and regulates expression of a resistance protein, coupled to the effects of the drug on cell growth and gene expression.
items.author: Geng, H., Schultz, D.

items.title: Identification of T-Cell specific signature miRNAs and target pathways in Psoriasis
items.summary: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by keratinocyte hyperproliferation, involving T cells as the major players in the manifestation of lesional and systemic inflammation. With the extensive exploration of keratinocyte dysfunctionality, T cell centric deregulation has gained much focus with limited molecular understanding in the context of disease etiology. miRNAs, the molecular switches known to drive disease manifestation via altering keratinocyte biology, have not been much studied in the context of T cell alterations. This study aims to explore T cell-associated miRNAs and their target signaling networks to understand their role in modulating psoriasis specific T cell changes. miRNAs with altered expression in psoriatic T cells were identified through a comprehensive analysis of the available literature and datasets.
items.author: Madaan, P., Tyagi, N., Tyagi, S. et al.

items.title: Dissociating Resting-State Networks of Pedohebephilic Preference and Child Sexual Offending Using Network-Based Prediction
items.summary: Pedohebephilia (P+), the sexual preference for prepubescent and early pubertal minors, regularly causes distress in those affected. While associated with child sexual offending (CSO), P+ is not a prerequisite for CSO. Limited neuroimaging studies have identified alterations associated with P+, while these may primarily reflect offending history. The correlates of P+ independent of CSO therefore remain unclear. We examined this distinction using intrinsic functional networks within a multivariate predictive framework. Using resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) and network-based prediction (NBS-Predict), we performed pairwise classifications among non-offending pedohebephilic men (P+CSO-, n=35), pedohebephilic men with CSO (P+CSO+, n=38), and non-pedohebephilic controls without CSO (P-CSO-, n=63).
items.author: Serin, E., Khan, K. R., Krueger, T. et al.

items.title: Sex differences in cell type-specific transcriptional programs and GPCR signaling in the human subgenual anterior cingulate cortex
items.summary: Psychiatric conditions show marked sex differences in disease onset, symptom presentation, and response to treatments. Understanding how sex differences manifest across molecularly distinct neuronal populations in individuals without psychiatric conditions may help explain sex-dependent variation in neural circuit function and treatment response. Here, we examined molecularly distinct cell types within the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) of non-psychiatric subjects. Using RNA sequencing data previously generated from laser-capture microdissected neurons, we investigated sex differences in gene expression and co-expression networks in excitatory pyramidal neurons (layers 2/3 and 5/6) and somatostatin (SST)-, parvalbumin (PVALB)-, and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing inhibitory interneurons (N=10 males, 9 females).
items.author: Snowden, A. W., Li, N. Y., Sibille, E. et al.

items.title: Temporal stability for individual differences in both habit learning and expression
items.summary: Actions transition from goal-directed to stimulus-driven habits through repetition. Individual differences in the capacity to learn and control habits are central to current models of psychopathology, which assume that overreliance on habitual control drives maladaptive behaviors. However, whether these tendencies reflect stable, trait-like cognitive processes remains unclear. We examined the temporal stability of individual differences in habit learning and expression. Across two preregistered experiments (total N = 313), we assessed stimulus-response habits using the same stimuli after one day or different stimuli after four months. Evidence for stable individual differences in habit commissions was strong and comparable across experiments, with computational modelling further supporting trait-like tendencies for habit learning and expression.
items.author: Martinez-Lopez, P., Leon, J. J., Garre-Frutos, F. et al.

items.title: The C. elegans Connectome Toolbox: an open, extensible framework for multimodal connectomic data integration and analysis
items.summary: The nematode C. elegans is one of the best studied model organisms in biology. Since the initial description of the C. elegans neuronal connectome by White and colleagues, numerous studies have mapped and analyzed the connectome, and released structured datasets of the connectivity, often merging and adding to previous versions. These datasets now serve as foundational resources that underpin studies into the neuronal basis of C. elegans behavior. In spite of their high utility, heterogeneity in the different datasets and their annotation conventions obscures direct comparison where discrepancies between connectomes frequently stem from differences in coverage or nomenclature rather than genuine biological disagreement.
items.author: Vickneswaran, Y., Ponzi, A., Sinha, A. et al.

items.title: 40 Hz visual stimulation increases gamma-band functional connectivity between visual, parietal and frontal regions
items.summary: Visual stimulation at 40 Hz is being investigated as a non-invasive intervention for Alzheimer's disease. Its neural responses have been reported in regions beyond the visual cortex, and concurrent cognitive tasks have been shown to increase their spatial extent. However, it is unclear whether these responses reflect increased functional connectivity between regions or a common response to the stimulus, and whether a concurrent task changes this connectivity. We recorded EEG from 29 healthy young adults during Regular 40 Hz flicker and Irregular 30-50 Hz flicker, each with and without a target-counting task (2 x 2 within-participant design). Source-space connectivity between visual, parietal, and frontal regions was estimated with the debiased squared weighted phase-lag index (dWPLI).
items.author: Ma, T., Sun, Q., Mlinaric, T. et al.

items.title: Social vision expands into auditory cortices of people born deaf: evidence from naturalistic film and encoding models
items.summary: Comparing deaf and hearing adults provides insight into the contribution of experience to function of auditory cortical networks. We used naturalistic fMRI and voxel-wise encoding to measure information processing in auditory networks of deaf (n=24) and hearing (n=22) adults who watched a 35-minute silent animated film. Unlike simpler stimuli, naturalistic films are rich in a broad range of perceptual, affective, and social features, including motion, dynamic social interactions, and Theory of Mind. Machine vision algorithms and human coding were used to densely annotate visual and social film features. In both groups we observed a right-lateralized processing hierarchy with encoding of low-level visual features in early visual areas, social visual features along the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and Theory of Mind in temporoparietal junction.
items.author: Zimmermann, M., Szwed, M., Isik, L. et al.

items.title: Increased activity without changes in coupling between somata and apical dendrites during visual mismatches
items.summary: Leading theories of cortical function posit that sensory processing involves a comparison between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory data. Tests of these theories have been hampered by experimental challenges related to simultaneously recording top-down and bottom-up signals in response to sensory stimuli that either do or do not match internally-generated predictions. Here, we conduct dual-plane 2-photon calcium imaging near-simultaneously from distal apical dendrites and somata of pyramidal neurons in each of 4 different regions of mouse visual cortex while the mice are presented with visual sequences that can either match or mismatch previously habituated visual stimuli. Specifically, we examine the responses in the distal apical dendrites and cell bodies of pyramidal neurons while mice view either movie clips that reverse unexpectedly or Gabor patch sequences that have orientations that do not match habituated patterns.
items.author: Henley, T. M., Tindall, J., Pina, J. E. et al.

items.title: Clonally Convergent Tph/Tfh-like CD4+ T Cells are Shared Across Recovery and Recurrence in Experimental Periodontitis
items.summary: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease of the tooth-supporting structures (periodontium) that requires life-long maintenance to prevent progression. Using a sensitized model of recurrent periodontitis in mice (SeRPD), in which regulatory breakdown was induced by temporary Treg depletion concurrent with disease, we mapped the gingival T cell imprint across each disease phase. Transient regulatory breakdown left a durable mucosal imprint after clinical recovery, characterized by enrichment of local and regional CD4 T cells. Paired single-cell RNA and TCR sequencing of gingival immune cells identified a convergent clonotype expanded from recovery into recurrence that carried a Tfh/Tph-like transcriptional identity. An analogous CD4 T cell population was detected in human periodontitis lesions by single-cell transcriptomics.
items.author: Sharma, A., Olmedo, V., Rojas, L. et al.

items.title: Temperature alters Culex tarsalis West Nile virus vector competence, tissue bottlenecks, and transcriptional responses
items.summary: West Nile virus is an arbovirus transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Temperature is frequently the strongest abiotic factor impacting transmission in many virus-vector pairings, including WNV and Culex. However, it is unknown how temperature impacts WNV population bottlenecks and transcriptional responses to infection in Culex tarsalis. We found that elevated temperatures led to increased likelihood of transmission of rare virus variants due to increased vector competence and less stringent tissue barriers. Analysis of Cx. tarsalis transcriptional responses confirmed that WNV infection had minimal impacts on transcriptional activity. Temperature, however, induced significant changes to mosquito gene expression, whereas canonical immune gene expression minimally changed in response to infection.
items.author: Gallichotte, E. N., King, D. C., Marsico, B. et al.

items.title: RNA Polymerase Backtracking Promotes Type III-A CRISPR DNA Targeting
items.summary: Type III CRISPR-Cas systems provide transcription-dependent immunity against mobile genetic elements, yet the mechanism underlying their DNA targeting remains unclear. Although the type III effector Cas10-Csm functions as a single-stranded DNase in vitro, type III systems eliminate double-stranded DNA targets in vivo, suggesting that transcription generates critical DNA substrates. Here, we show that conserved RNA polymerase anti-backtracking factors, such as GreA, selectively inhibit DNA-targeting of type III immunity. GreA overexpression abolishes protection against both phages and conjugative plasmids, whereas mutations that disrupt GreA anti-backtracking activity eliminate this effect. In contrast, immunity mediated by the type II CRISPR-Cas system or the auxiliary type III RNase Csm6 remain unaffected, demonstrating that GreA specifically suppresses Cas10-dependent DNA interference.
items.author: Hernandez Viera, A. J., Gross, N. R., Tran, P. Q. et al.

items.title: Phage lysates are reservoirs of biologically active quorum sensing signals
items.summary: Bacteriophage lysates are widely used to study phage-bacterial interactions and are typically applied after filtration without further purification. As a result, host-derived metabolites produced during phage propagation are transferred alongside phage particles, yet the biological consequences of this carryover remain largely unexplored. Here, we show that the Pseudomonas aeruginosa quorum sensing signal PQS persists in a bioactive state in phage lysates for at least one year. In contrast, the quorum sensing molecules 3OC12-HSL and C4-HSL are rapidly degraded. We demonstrate that PQS stability is caused by its association with outer membrane vesicles, which protect the signal from degradation. PQS from phage lysates induces production of the virulence factor pyocyanin and increases mortality in a Galleria mellonella model of P.
items.author: Eichler, A. H., Mauritzen, J. J., Koonce, K. C. et al.

items.title: Pneumocystis phosphoglucomutase links glucose-phosphate metabolism to β-1,3-glucan synthesis and cell-wall integrity
items.summary: The fungal cell wall is a dynamic, carbohydrate-rich structure whose composition is closely coordinated with cellular metabolism. Phosphoglucomutase (PGM) interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking carbon metabolism with UDP-glucose-dependent cell-wall biosynthesis. We previously identified functional Pgm2 homologs from Pneumocystis jirovecii and Pneumocystis murina. Here, using a Saccharomyces cerevisiae pgm2{Delta} complementation model, we examined the relationship between Pgm2 activity, {beta}-1,3-glucan, and cell-wall integrity. Pgm2 deficiency reduced {beta}-1,3-glucan content and altered zymolyase sensitivity without major changes in cell-wall thickness. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed that the pgm2{Delta} mutant exhibited coordinated metabolic and cell-wall transcriptional responses, including increased SLT2/MPK1, RLM1, FKS2/GSC2, GFA1, CHS1, CRH1, SED1, and CWP1 expression and decreased FKS1, GAS1, GAS3, and CHS2 expression.
items.author: Kottom, T., McLean, J. L., Limper, A. H.

items.title: Optimal compositions of potent sliced-siRNA with DNA bases substitution and insights of Ago2 slicing actions
items.summary: We have previously characterized the nucleotide compositions of single-stranded ago2-sliced small interfering RNAs (sliced-siRNA, sliRNA), a novel type of potent RNAi trigger designed based on the biogenesis mechanism of miRNA-451. sliRNAs have on par antisense mediated silencing activity but about 1000-fold reduced passenger strand activity compared to siRNA. In the current study, to further characterize sliRNAs to facilitate their in vivo application, we have investigated the effects of substituting RNA nucleotides (nts) in sliRNA with DNA nts (sliDRNAs), which will allow us to study the potential effects on their processing, maturation, and silencing activity from individual or multiple nts at different positions.
items.author: Sun, G., Lizhar, E. M., Shi, Y. et al.

items.title: Insulin stimulation induces dynamic interaction between 14-3-3 and the C-terminal tail domain of Kinesin-2 subunit KIF3B in vitro
items.summary: Heterotrimeric kinesin[ndash]2 mediates diverse intracellular transport processes, yet the mechanisms governing its cargo specificity and regulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we report the regulation of interaction between the kinesin[ndash]2 subunit KIF3B and a candidate adaptor protein, 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon];. Using splitAPEX2 proximity labelling and fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) assays in HEK293T cells, we demonstrate that 14[ndash]3[ndash]3[epsilon]; interacts with KIF3B within discrete subcellular compartments. This interaction is significantly enhanced upon insulin stimulation, indicating regulation by signalling pathways. Time resolved FLIM analysis further reveals that the site of interaction is dynamic, suggesting spatial and temporal control of motora[ndash]daptor association. Finally, the interactions are mapped to two serine residues in the C[ndash]terminal tail region of KIF3B that are highly conserved across species.
items.author: Kumari, D., Tangri, A., Girotra, M. et al.

items.title: N-terminal cysteine independent effects of oxidative stress on the stability of RGS4 and 5
items.summary: Oxidative post-translational modifications on the sulfhydryl group of cysteines can occur spontaneously or enzymatically. The enzymatic dioxygenation of N-terminal cysteines has emerged as a new oxygen sensing paradigm, catalysed by 2-aminoethanethiol dioxygenase (ADO) in mammals. Conflicting evidence has been reported in recent years on whether this reaction can occur spontaneously in the absence of ADO. Here we sought to address whether cellular oxidative stress can interfere with ADO-catalysed N-terminal cysteine dioxygenation. Using a system to produce titratable intracellular levels of H2O2, we demonstrate that the stability of RGS4 and 5 is not affected by physiological levels of oxidative stress, whether ADO is present or not.
items.author: Kim, H., Shang, N., Tian, Y.-M. et al.

items.title: Variation in the embryonic cell lineages of Caenorhabditis elegans natural populations
items.summary: Developmental variation has often been appreciated as a major phenotypic substrate of evolutionary innovation in multicellular organisms. Although quantification of developmental variation in isogenic populations has a long history, it has been difficult to accomplish across natural populations until recently. Given its invariant cell lineage, Caenorhabditis elegans represents an ideal model system for studying how natural diversity in development is expressed at the resolution of single cells, cell lineages, and the whole embryo. Using embGAN, a deep-learning pipeline that enables label-free lineage tracing without the bottleneck and potential confounding effects of generating transgenic strains, we reconstructed the early embryonic lineage of 78 embryos spanning eight genetic backgrounds, including six wild strains, and quantified cell-cycle timing with a lineage-aligned graph metric that separates global rescaling of developmental rate from localized changes in lineage structure.
items.author: Weymer, C., Johnson, R. L., Helou, J. O. et al.

items.title: Phenotypic Plasticity in Sub-Antarctic Plants: Costs, Environmental Complexity, and the Facilitative Role of Trait Integration
items.summary: Phenotypic plasticity is one plant response to climate warming, but it may incur costs and be either limited or facilitated by trait integration or simultaneous environmental shifts such as shading. Empirical studies addressing these costs and limitations across populations or maternal lineages, and how they vary with environmental context, remain scarce. We studied three plant species from the sub-Antarctic Kerguelen Islands, a region undergoing rapid warming, growing seeds from multiple source populations under different temperature and light treatments. We measured plasticity, performance, and morphological integration in young plants. Plants from more plastic source populations performed worse, while those from more integrated populations were more plastic, consistent with the facilitation hypothesis.
items.author: Hennion, F., Labarrere, B., Renaudon, M. et al.

items.title: A timeline for evolution of metabolism in early microbes
items.summary: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4 billion years ago (Ga) with fermentation and sulfur compound respiration. A second wave began ~3.2 Ga with aerobic respiration and growth, while a third began ~1.4 Ga with further specialization. We compared these predictions with independent dates from the geochemical record, and agreement with conservative dates was good (CCC = 0.81 to 0.89).
items.author: Hackmann, T.

items.title: How Fisherian runaway halts: Genomic architecture determines the long-term evolutionary consequences of sexual selection.
items.summary: Sexual selection explains the evolution of exaggerated sexual displays, but less obvious is why biased mate preferences--a requirement for sexual selection--evolve. Fisher (1930) proposed that biased mate preferences can spark self-reinforcing evolutionary process (runaway) that drives their own evolution. This occurs because mate choice imposes sexual selection on sexual displays and links them genetically to mate preferences, producing indirect selection on the preferences themselves. While mathematical models have demonstrated the plausibility of the runaway theory, they rely on several idealized assumptions. Consequently, it remains poorly understood how runaway halts once populations deviate from these idealized conditions as a consequence of evolution via runaway, and how the genetic architecture underlying sexual displays influences the resulting evolutionary dynamics.
items.author: Kagawa, K., Kawata, M.

items.title: Short-read whole-genome sequencing identifies the Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg transgene insertion site on mouse chromosome 4
items.summary: Tg(Tal1-cre/ERT)42-056Jrg, also known as HSC-Scl-CreERT, is a well-used transgenic allele that enables genetic manipulation in mouse hematopoietic cells. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing, we identified the transgene insertion site on chromosome 4 approximately 6 kb upstream of Echdc2.

items.title: Auditing Biomedical Literature with Blinded AI Peer Review: Where Peer Review Works, Where It Fails, and How to Strengthen It
items.summary: Biomedical publishing has grown more than elevenfold since 1991, outstripping human peer review. Unblinded language models cannot audit this literature objectively because they recognize famous authors and journals from training memory. We built BARS (Blinded AI Review System), an automated referee that strips titles, author names, institutions, journal headers, and dates before grading full-text manuscripts on a 10-point scale covering methods, evidence, biology, and reproducibility. We used BARS to generate 1,874 blind reviews across 1,714 unique papers. BARS passed 100% of verified sound controls, caught 77% to 91% of internally flawed papers, eliminated a +0.35-point prestige boost, and more than doubled human referee consistency.
items.author: Kosakovsky Pond, S. L., Pond, S. J. K., Weaver, S. et al.

items.title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
items.summary: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex.
items.author: Nickerson, E., Pomeroy-Tuck, J., Pratt, S. et al.

items.title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
items.summary: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2).
items.author: Qu, C., Naeve, C., Shi, Z.

items.title: Mitochondria-Coupled Hitchhiking Drives Vimentin Intermediate Filament Transport
items.summary: Vimentin intermediate filaments (VIFs) undergo active microtubule-dependent transport throughout the cell, with trajectories resembling those of motor-driven organelles, yet our recent work showed that only a small subset of VIFs lies close to microtubules. How VIFs engage the microtubule-based transport machinery, and whether additional transport routes contribute, remain unresolved. We hypothesized that VIFs move indirectly, by hitchhiking on motile organelles, and tested this using mitochondria. Live imaging showed mitochondria and adjacent VIFs moving together, and volume electron microscopy revealed VIFs closely following mitochondrial surfaces at sites distinct from microtubule contacts. Depleting the mitochondrial motor adaptor TRAK1 to inhibit anterograde mitochondrial transport shifted both mitochondria and VIFs toward the nucleus.
items.author: Renganathan, B., Moore, A. S., Adam, S. A. et al.

items.title: Sex-specific bone marrow populations regulate skeletal phenotype and identify CD74-marked osteoclast precursor subsets
items.summary: While there are clear differences in bone accrual and maintenance between men and women due to hormonal regulation, the potential cell-intrinsic factors governing this difference are poorly understood. To investigate this, we performed bone marrow transplantation assays using male or female bone marrow transplantation into male hosts. Micro-CT analyses of lethally irradiated 8-week-old male mice transplanted with female bone marrow exhibited increased vertebral body trabecular and cortical bone mass. To identify cell types mediating these effects, we performed comparative single cell sequencing analyses and identified several CD11B+CD74+ myeloid cell clusters. Male donor BM chimeric mice had a higher proportion of Cd74-expressing clusters compared to female donor BM chimeric mice.
items.author: Koroth, J., Karkache, I. Y., Vu, E. K. et al.

items.title: PPI-Rescue: restoration of eye development via functional reconstitution of a transcription complex.
items.summary: The activity of transcription factors (TFs) can be modulated through protein-protein interactions (PPIs) with cofactors which can serve to enhance, repress or alter the specificity of TF function. Current genetic and molecular approaches such as knockout and overexpression studies are likely to affect all possible activities of a TF, presenting a dilemma when attempting to parse out how TFs function within a cell. Hence, there is a need to devise a technique that will allow for mechanistic insight to be gained into the function(s) of discrete transcription complexes. Herein we report ''PPI-Rescue'', an approach that leverages bespoke mutations in TFs and the selective reconstitution of specific complexes to study the molecular properties and biological functions of discrete transcription complexes in vitro and in vivo.
items.author: Jusic, N., Pina, C., Netz, D. et al.

items.title: Habitat degradation destabilizes complex metacommunities by disrupting dispersal
items.summary: Habitat loss and fragmentation are rapidly reshaping ecosystems worldwide, yet their consequences for ecological stability remain unresolved. Classical theory, pioneered by Robert May, established rigorous criteria for stability; however, these apply to spatially well-mixed communities, limiting their relevance to habitat degradation. Here, we develop a metacommunity framework that integrates classical stability theory with spatial dynamics to determine how anthropogenic habitat degradation reshapes ecosystem stability. We show that metacommunities exhibit three distinct dynamical regimes following a perturbation (e.g., drought or forest fire): stable regime (perturbations decay and species persist), reactive regime (perturbations are transiently amplified, which increases extinction risk under repeated disturbances), and unstable regime (perturbations grow, causing extinctions even after a single disturbance).
items.author: Sun, Y., Yin, X., Jin, Z. et al.

items.title: Protein language models learn the underlying accessibility of mutations alongside protein fitness landscapes
items.summary: Protein language models (PLMs) score the effects of amino acid replacements as pseudo-probabilities, which are widely utilised to map protein fitness landscapes. However, because their training data relies on natural amino acid sequences, these models conflate protein structural constraints with nucleotide mutation biases and codon accessibility. Using the rapid emergence of the divergent influenza A H3N2 K lineage as a stress test, we investigate how base PLMs (ESM-2 and ESM-C) versus fine-tuned versions of these models capture mutational processes. We systematically implement a parameter sweep to explicitly couple (or decouple) empirical nucleotide mutational supply from PLM-assessed amino acid substitution pseudo-probabilities across evolutionary forecasting tasks.
items.author: MacLean, O. A., Lamb, K., Lytras, S. et al.

items.title: Novel Regulators of Sugar-dependent Food Consumption in Drosophila melanogaster
items.summary: Diet and genetic background interact to influence food consumption, yet the genetic basis of diet-dependent feeding behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we used genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) to investigate the genetic regulation of sugar-dependent food consumption in Drosophila melanogaster. Food intake was quantified in 176 lines of the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) using the Con-Ex (Consumption-Excretion) assay on low- and high-sugar foods. Flies showed compensatory feeding, consuming more low-sugar food than high-sugar food, and this behavior was largely maintained across genotypes. Additionally, the magnitude and overall consumption varied several-fold among lines, with broad-sense heritability of 0.53 to 0.66 across sexes and diets.
items.author: Opoola, M. A., Fitzgerald, L., Ahmed, S. et al.

items.title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
items.summary: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment.
items.author: Cantat, A., Guerin, C., Morel, N. et al.

items.title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
items.summary: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.
items.author: Tian, Y., Zhou, Q., Yu, Q. et al.

items.title: Bicarbonate-free pH neutralization resensitizes ovarian cancer to chemotherapy and is tracked by 3T CEST MRI
items.summary: Ovarian tumors that initially respond to platinum-taxane chemotherapy often relapse as chemoresistant disease. The acidic tumor microenvironment is a well-known but under-exploited driver of this resistance, and neutralization strategies such as oral bicarbonate have not translated. Here we show that inhibiting specific tumor pH regulators at noncytotoxic doses relieves acidosis and restores frontline chemotherapy, monitored noninvasively at clinical 3T. In OVCAR3 and SKOV-3 ovarian cancer cells, MCT1 and MCT4 were overexpressed under acidosis, and the MCT4 inhibitor acriflavine reduced extracellular acidification at concentrations well below its cytotoxic IC50, without bicarbonate buffering. Acidosis blunted the efficacy of both paclitaxel and carboplatin, raising their IC50 values, which acriflavine reversed.
items.author: Patkulkar, P. A., Mandal, A., Noble, S. et al.

items.title: Transferrin receptor binding valency determines the circulating half-life and weight-loss efficacy of Fc-FGF21 in TfR-humanized mice
items.summary: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is a promising metabolic hormone with potent anti-obesity effects. It acts in both the central nervous system and peripheral tissues to exert its metabolic benefits. Because its receptors are expressed at low levels in the brain, we hypothesized that enhanced transport across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) would improve its efficacy. To achieve this, FGF21 was fused to Fc(TV35), an engineered Fc fragment that binds the human transferrin receptor (hTfR), to generate Fc(TV35)-FGF21. Fc(TV35)-FGF21 does not bind to mouse TfR, so it produced weight-loss effects in wild-type diet-induced obese mice comparable to those of Fc-FGF21. However, it failed to induce weight loss in homozygous hTfR-humanized mice because of a markedly shortened circulating half-life.
items.author: Zhou, H., Deng, Y., Li, H. et al.

items.title: Live Droplet Single-Cell RNA Sequencing
items.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing has emerged as one of the most influential methods of the past decade, enabling the dissection of cellular heterogeneity and the discovery of rare cell types. However, most workflows require cell lysis and provide only terminal snapshots, limiting their ability to capture dynamic cellular trajectories and temporal variations within the same cell. Herein, we present Live Droplet single-cell RNA sequencing (Live D-seq), a technology that enables scalable transcriptome-wide profiling of individual living cells over time. Live D-seq combines longitudinal intracellular sampling of live, barcoded cells with particle-templated emulsification and barcoded hydrogel beads, enabling repeated samples from the same cell lineage to be linked across time points.
items.author: Reynolds, D. E., Lee, S., Oh, D. et al.

items.title: Adaptation of breast cancer cells to serum-free defined medium reveals changes in proliferation, adhesion, and lipid metabolism
items.summary: Cancer cell metabolic dependencies are strongly influenced by nutrient availability, yet conventional culture conditions contain non-physiological nutrient concentrations and poorly defined serum components that may obscure metabolic vulnerabilities. Here, we investigated the adaptation of three breast cancer cell lines to physiologically relevant, serum-free defined medium (DM). Using a stepwise reduction in fetal bovine serum (FBS), we evaluated proliferation, adhesion, morphology, and transcriptional changes in HER2-positive SK-BR-3, triple-negative MDA-MB-231, and ER-positive/HER2-positive BT-474 cells. The three cell lines differed substantially in their ability to adapt to serum-free conditions. MDA-MB-231 cells adapted readily, maintaining proliferation and adhesion without exogenous substrate coatings. SK-BR-3 cells also achieved sustained proliferation in serum-free DM, but required a serum-derived coating to maintain adhesion.
items.author: Aarrestad, C., Khatib, T. O., Alvarez, J. V.

items.title: Lineage tracing in rhabdoid tumor organoids and orthotopic xenografts reveals convergent transcriptional states
items.summary: Malignant rhabdoid tumors (MRTs) are aggressive pediatric malignancies driven by loss of a single SWI/SNF subunit in an otherwise near-silent genome, yet they display extensive transcriptional heterogeneity. Whether this heterogeneity reflects the outgrowth of transcriptionally distinct clones, or states adopted independently of lineage, is unknown. Here we combined lentiviral lineage barcoding with single-cell RNA sequencing in two patient-derived renal MRT organoid models, followed through long-term in vitro culture and in a novel orthotopic xenograft setting. In both modalities, tumors and cultures became progressively restricted to a small number of lineages, and the clones that expanded were transcriptionally distinct from one another.
items.author: Perticari, G., DeMartino, J., Fumagalli, A. et al.

items.title: Histopathological and virus-associated features of Boid Inclusion Body Disease in Boa constrictor
items.summary: Boid inclusion body disease (BIBD) is a reptarenavirus-induced fatal disease of boid snakes that, while diagnosed with ease due to the pathognomonic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (IB), is not yet fully characterized pathomorphologically and with regards to its pathogenesis. The present study retrospectively investigated a random cohort of 50 captive male and female boa constrictors of variable age (neonate to 25 years) for histopathological changes and in situ viral protein (nucleoprotein, NP, and glycoprotein 2, GP2) expression patterns. IB formation and NP expression were scored semiquantitatively. The vast majority of snakes (42/50; 84%) exhibited histopathological changes; these mainly (39/42; 93%) represented inflammatory processes that most frequently affected the gastrointestinal tract.
items.author: Bogner, M., Dervas, E., De Neck, S. et al.

items.title: Vorinostat Can Reduce an Ongoing Fibrosis and Preserve Key Liver Metabolic Functions by Selectively Altering Mesenchymal Cell Differentiation
items.summary: Liver fibrosis is a major global cause of mortality that is driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) into extracellular matrix (ECM)-producing myofibroblasts (MyoFs). The lack of predictive human in vitro models has severely hampered the discovery of targeted anti-fibrotic therapies. Here, we describe a human iPSC-derived hepatic micro-organoid (microHO) model, which labels collagen producing cells, to study liver fibrosis pathophysiology and screen drug candidates. We discovered that while multiple drugs prevented fibrosis when co-administered prophylactically with TGF{beta}1, only the FDA-approved pan-HDAC inhibitor Vorinostat (SAHA) successfully reduced an established, ongoing fibrosis and preserved life-sustaining liver metabolic functions in a fibrotic microenvironment, including ammonia detoxification and CYP3A4-mediated drug metabolism.
items.author: GUAN, Y., Peltz, G.

items.title: Site-, strain- and mutation-specific osteopetrosis phenotypes in mice with Clcn7 variants
items.summary: Background: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (ADOII) is a rare bone disorder caused primarily by heterozygous mutations in CLCN7 and characterized by increased bone mass yet fragility and marked phenotypic heterogeneity among affected individuals. The biological factors underlying this variability remain poorly understood. We investigated the effects of age, sex, genetic background, and mutation type on bone phenotypes in murine models of ADOII carrying heterozygous Clcn7 F318L/+ or G213R/+ mutations. Methods: Bone microarchitecture was assessed by micro-computed tomography in vertebrae and femora from female and male mice across multiple ages (12, 24, and 52 weeks) and strain backgrounds (FVB/NJ, C57BL/6, and 129).
items.author: Shimonty, A., Dahl, X. G., Zboinski, E. et al.

items.title: The chloroplast-localised transporter RETICULATA controls palisade mesophyll cell division and expansion
items.summary: Plant leaves contain extensive intercellular air spaces, which contribute to photosynthetic capacity and water use efficiency in different environments. Despite this importance, the developmental mechanisms that control leaf air space patterning are poorly understood. For over 20 years it has been known that plants with disrupted chloroplast biogenesis and metabolism have increased intercellular air spaces, but the underlying molecular mechanism is unknown. Here, we characterise leaf air space morphogenesis in mutants of the chloroplast amino acid transporter RETICULATA (RE), which has enlarged air spaces. We show that the reticulata-6 (re-6) loss of function mutant exhibits increased air space expansion specifically in the palisade, and not the spongy, mesophyll.
items.author: Locke Bevia, E. A., Aldorino, E., Fitzsimons, J. M. et al.

items.title: Anionic lipids stabilize etioplast prolamellar bodies and facilitate thylakoid biogenesis during etioplast-to-chloroplast differentiation
items.summary: Etioplasts of dark-grown angiosperm seedlings contain prolamellar bodies (PLBs), lattice-like membranes that are quickly transformed into thylakoids upon illumination. Phosphatidylglycerol (PG) and sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol (SQDG) are major anionic lipids in these membranes, but their roles in etioplast-to-chloroplast differentiation remain unclear. We analyzed Arabidopsis thaliana mutants with reduced PG biosynthesis (pgp1-1), complete SQDG deficiency (sqd1), and the pgp1-1 sqd1 double mutant. Although pgp1-1 etioplasts showed a loosened PLB lattice when fixed under white light, they retained regular, wild-type-like lattices when fixed under infrared light, suggesting that their PLBs were more susceptible to light-induced disassembly. The rapid PLB disassembly in pgp1-1 upon illumination was accompanied by rapid conversion of dark-accumulated protochlorophyllide to chlorophyll and lamellar membrane formation, suggesting a link between membrane remodeling and chlorophyll formation.
items.author: Yoshihara, A., Uwatoko, R., Kobayashi, K. et al.

items.title: Consequence and further analysis of the minor role of daylength in the floral initiation of sorghum crops
items.summary: Background and Aims Flowering time is assumed to be primarily controlled by daylength, but field observations disagree. For instance, mid-early sorghum varieties sown at the same time at tropical and temperate latitudes have similar flowering dates. We previously proposed an alternative framework integrating daily changes in sunrise and sunset times (dSR and dSS). Methods Variety trials of mid-late varieties from the Northern Hemisphere were carried out in Madagascar and in Argentina. Series of monthly sowings of 28 varieties were carried out in Mali between 2000 and 2009. Heading date and, in Mali, panicle initiation (PI) were recorded. Key Results In Madagascar and in Argentina mid-late varieties headed late or very late when sown in November and December, consistent with the higher dSR/dSS values of the southern hemisphere summer.
items.author: Clerget, B., Sidibe, M., vom Brocke, K. et al.

items.title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
items.summary: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered.
items.author: Mugglestone, S., Hughes, S. W., Ganis, G.

items.title: Automated Segmentation of the Hypothalamus: Associations of Age and Socioeconomic Status with Subunit Volumes in Cognitively Healthy Adults
items.summary: Background: The hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake cycles, energy balance, and autonomic and neuroendocrine function, yet its small size and poorly contrasted boundaries have long hindered in vivo volumetry. Deep-learning segmentation now allows the hypothalamus to be divided into functionally meaningful subunits. We examined whether hypothalamic subunit volumes are associated with age and socioeconomic status (SES) in cognitively healthy adults. Methods: From the OASIS-1 cross-sectional dataset (n = 416, 18-96 years), 133 participants with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0 and complete segmentation output were analysed (33-94 years). A FreeSurfer-based convolutional neural network, run on a cloud virtual machine, segmented five subunits per hemisphere.
items.author: Akar, B., Atasever, U.

items.title: Gain Control of Peripheral Input by Core Brain Thermosensors Drives Drosophila Thermoregulation
items.summary: Temperature affects all aspects of animal physiology, rendering thermoregulation critical for survival. In Drosophila larvae, well-established peripheral thermosensors detect temperature changes and mediate thermotaxis over a broad innocuous range, but how larvae seek a specific preferred body temperature within this range remains unknown. Here we show that core thermosensors in the brain (LPBT neurons) establish this setpoint by mediating warming-evoked turning at temperatures above it. LPBTs express the warmth-activated thermosensor TrpA1(A), but are not simply cell-autonomous thermosensors. Rather, sustained LPBT responses above setpoint require both peripheral thermosensory input and TRPA1-dependent thermosensing within LPBTs. TRPA1-dependent core thermosensing provides gain control that defines the homeostatic setpoint by tuning the behavioral weights of peripheral inputs.
items.author: Lazopulo, S., Zlatic, M., Cardona, A. et al.

items.title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
items.summary: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability.
items.author: GUO, X., Leong, Y. C., Bainbridge, W. A.

items.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
items.summary: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives.
items.author: Minasi, C. B., Hassan, U., Cline, C. C. et al.

items.title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
items.summary: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes.
items.author: Brody, D. L., Dengler, B. A., Angelo, J. P. et al.

items.title: Intra-individual changes to peak alpha frequency map to pain perception following high frequency sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
items.summary: Resting-state EEG can capture cortical dynamics relevant to sensitised pain states in the absence of ongoing nociceptive engagement. However, whilst the slowing of global oscillations is evident within various chronic pain conditions, the mechanistic specificity of PAF and -band power remains uncertain. Therefore, the present study assessed these features across two identical test-retest sessions in which HFS was applied to induce the development of SHA as characterised through 128 mN MPS. Crucially, changes in -band features post-HFS were investigated. Blind source separation was also applied to identify independent sensorimotor components relevant to nociception and assess their test-retest reliability. Results demonstrated good test-retest reliability for sensor-level data at baseline, with inter-individual changes in global PAF reflecting MPS post-HFS.
items.author: Mugglestone, S., Hughes, S. W., Ganis, G.

items.title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
items.summary: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output.
